issue: In a prosecution under the Indian Country Crimes Act, must the government plead and prove the defendant's non-Indian status (and the absence of tribal punishment or a treaty exception) as an element of the offense, or is the defendant's Indian status an affirmative defense that the defendant must first raise?

sides.position: Non-Indian status is an affirmative defense: the defendant must first properly raise the issue (and the enumerated exceptions), after which the government bears the ultimate burden of proof.
cases: United States v. Hester, 719 F.2d 1040 (9th Cir. 1983)
United States v. Haggerty, 997 F.3d 292 (5th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Webster, 797 F.3d 531 (8th Cir. 2015)
United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. 2026)

sides.position: Non-Indian status is an element of the offense that the government must prove at trial, as established by the en banc Tenth Circuit decision.
cases: United States v. Prentiss, 256 F.3d 971 (10th Cir. 2001) (en banc)
United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. 2026)

this_court: Tenth Circuit treats non-Indian status as an element and follows Prentiss, while acknowledging the contrary view and urging en banc reexamination; it does not overrule Prentiss.
quote: The American Indian Law in a Nutshell, a comprehensive resource on the federal law of American Indians, cognizes the circuit split. William C. Canby, Jr., American Indian Law in a Nutshell 195 (Jesse E. Chopper et al. eds., 8th ed. 2025) (“Circuits have split on the question whether the Indian or non-Indian status of the defendant must be pleaded and proved by the government in a prosecution under 18 U.S.C.A. § 1152.”).
cite: United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. 2026)
